claims.text: The starting catalyst is a nearly equiatomic, multi-element automotive alloy with low platinum-group-metal content.
The untreated catalyst loses activity and durability during transient exhaust operation and thermal aging.
Sintering contributes to degradation of the untreated catalyst.
Poisoning, including effects associated with H2O and NO exposure, contributes to degradation of the untreated catalyst.
ALD at 150–200 °C with controlled cycle counts can produce a conformal, uniform 1–2 nm CeO2 overlayer on the catalyst.
Calcination in air at approximately 400 °C will ensure strong overlayer adhesion without excessive film growth.
The treatment will form a tightly bonded CeO2 shell that directly interfaces with low-loading PGM sites.
CeO2 acts as an oxygen storage and release medium and as a redox mediator.
High oxygen mobility in the CeO2 overlayer buffers the catalyst against transient oxidizing and reducing conditions.
The CeO2 overlayer protects active PGM sites from sintering.
The CeO2 overlayer protects active PGM sites from poisoning by H2O and NO.
The CeO2 overlayer enhances redox kinetics needed to sustain catalytic turnover at low temperature.
The CeO2-overlayered catalyst will have improved low-temperature catalytic activity relative to the untreated catalyst.
The CeO2-overlayered catalyst will have superior durability during extended transient exhaust operation and thermal aging.
The CeO2 treatment will reduce catalyst deactivation relative to the untreated catalyst.
Adding the CeO2 overlayer will not increase platinum-group-metal consumption.
An excessively thick or non-uniform CeO2 layer could block access to active sites.
Insufficient CeO2 coverage may fail to provide the proposed protection.
Optimal performance is expected in transient, low-temperature gasoline or hybrid exhaust containing typical H2O and NO exposures.
